rv.q: "It deals with powerful themes of guilt and responsibility, tautly dramatized and well-defined. But the play is also talky and didactic, its themes expressed too baldly…Still, the brief work has a gripping cumulative power that builds to a surprising conclusion, which is at once uplifting and tragic.
Miller's answer here may strain credibility, but he certainly asked the right questions.
But as the respectable if sometimes stolid revival that opened on Sunday at the Signature Theater reveals, the passing of the decades has perhaps inevitably dimmed the play’s power.
Unfortunately, the current production, directed by Michael Wilson, only reaches that level a few times during its swift 90 minutes.
Michael Wilson, lately of 'The Trip to Bountiful,' ratchets up the dramatic tension much higher than you'd think it could possibly go, and his ensemble cast is superior.
This is a discussion play in which the discussion is ultimately quite one-sided, which gives the play, which is meant to be searching, a kind of complacency.
This production, though sometimes stirring, helps illustrate why.

Off-Broadway’s Signature Theatre Company is currently presenting a superb, highly compelling revival of Miller’s rarely-performed one-act Holocaust drama “Incident at Vichy,” which was first produced in 1964.
For better and worse, “Incident at Vichy” proves to be another one well worth heeding.
This production serves Arthur Miller admirably.
It can be an uncomfortable play to watch, but it's the discomfort that makes it good theatre.
Even if a few things about this production don't fully work, it remains a vivid account of the administration of savagery as practiced in a not-too-distant time.
If it’s the well-spoken Pettie who explains why we’re here, it’s Thomas and Carpinello whose performances force “Vichy” into more active territory.
Incident at Vichy...is intelligent, well acted, and occasionally so relevant that it's chilling.
Not the case with this production of Incident at Vichy, which even so is recommended as an opportunity to catch a sturdy production of one of Miller's mid-level plays.
Wilson’s faithful, by-the-book staging, however impressive, does little to offset the feeling that we’re watching an elaborately decorated college seminar.
And also, “Incident at Vichy” is one of his weaker efforts, which director Michael Wilson‘s production makes abundantly clear.
They succeed as neither endeavor.
Out of actual events, the playwright’s shaping purpose created a powerful work of art.
The 90 minute, no intermission, work is chilling in it’s dramatic intent as it grips the audience in tragic events that will never be forgotten.
Arthur Miller’s 1964 examination of the Holocaust as it played out in France is, like all of his best work, a tragedy you can’t look away from.

In Incident At Vichy, Miller wants each and every theatergoer to ask oneself: how much are you willing to sacrifice to stop something you know is wrong, and will you make that sacrifice before it's too late?
But, under the unsteady direction of Michael Wilson, the acting is more of a mixed bag in the new Signature production.
Unfortunately it’s not also a very gripping one.
On the whole, I loved seeing Incident at Vichy.
Nonetheless INCIDENT AT VICHY is worth seeing. The arguments are timely and the performances are excellent.

cn.t: Miller's rarely-revived Holocaust drama receives a well-acted, thoughtful production, though critics find the play itself heavy-handed and overly didactic, with worthy themes undermined by lengthy speeches and lack of nuance.
